```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(rMVPA)
```

## What a matched similarity measures

A pattern can resemble its matched partner because the template resembles
retrieval patterns generally, because the retrieval pattern resembles templates
generally, or because that particular pair exceeds both tendencies. All three
can covary with a rating such as vividness. Endpoint tendencies can carry
meaningful stimulus or state information; they are not causal directions or
automatically noise.

`era_endpoint_decomposition()` separates these terms within prespecified,
complete competitor blocks. **Encoding/templates are rows; retrieval patterns
are columns.** After centering each pattern across voxels and normalizing its
length, the cross-product matrix contains spatial Pearson similarities. Within
each block, using only nonmatches, the model is

\[
M_{ij}=\mu+a_i+b_j+\epsilon_{ij},\quad i\ne j,\qquad
\sum_i a_i=\sum_i b_i=0.
\]

The diagonal is then decomposed as
\(d_i=\mu+a_i+b_i+e_i\). The shared baseline is \(\mu\), the encoding/template
endpoint is \(a_i\), the retrieval endpoint is \(b_i\), and matched excess is
\(e_i\). Endpoints never use the diagonal. This is an exact joint least-squares
fit, including its finite-block correction, rather than two independently
subtracted backgrounds. It requires at least three matched items per block.

```{r standalone}
set.seed(92)
keys <- sprintf("item%02d", 1:12)
E <- matrix(rnorm(12 * 20), 12, dimnames = list(keys, NULL))
R <- E + matrix(rnorm(12 * 20), 12)
rownames(R) <- keys
enc_run <- setNames(rep(c("E1", "E2"), each = 6), keys)
ret_run <- setNames(rep(c("R1", "R2"), each = 6), keys)
pool <- setNames(as.character(interaction(enc_run, ret_run, drop = TRUE)), keys)

z <- era_endpoint_decomposition(
  E, R, competitor_block = pool,
  encoding_run = enc_run, retrieval_run = ret_run
)
head(z$items)
z$blocks
```

Keys are mandatory, either as matrix row names or explicit `item_key`. Separate
encoding and retrieval key vectors can be supplied in a named list. Retrieval
rows are reordered by identity, never paired by unlabelled row order. Metadata
vectors can be named by key. Unnamed metadata must have exactly one value per
declared key; scalar recycling, repeated-item averaging, and incomplete key
matching are refused. Feature columns must have matching identities and order.
Phase-scoped run labels are recorded separately from the declared competitor
pool; run labels alone do not determine the pool.

Nonfinite or constant spatial patterns invalidate their **entire block**. The
returned NA components and `status` explain why. `invalid = "error"` requests a
hard failure. No items are silently removed and no correlations use different
voxel subsets for different pairs. Weighted, rectangular and incomplete
competitor designs require a generalized solver and are unsupported here.
Unusable small blocks are retained in the denominator/exclusion ledger.

The default pattern path uses normalized pattern sums. Set
`return_matrices = TRUE` to retain the explicit within-block matrices, or supply
`similarity_matrix` to decompose already computed, pre-link scores. The latter
does not certify that arbitrary matrices can be realized as spatial correlations.
Probability, softmax, rank-percentile and correctness outputs remain separate:
the linear decomposition does not carry through those nonlinear operations.

## Specificity and excess are different trial scores

Existing retrieval-column specificity is
\(s_i=d_i-\operatorname{mean}_{j\ne i}M_{ji}\). For a complete block of size n,

\[
s_i=\frac{n}{n-1}a_i+e_i.
\]

It removes the retrieval endpoint and retains the template endpoint. Its
correlation with behavior is therefore a different estimand from the excess
correlation. Existing `matched`, `background`, `specificity`, `era_diag_minus_off`
and feature metrics keep their meanings. `era_partition_model()` also remains
distinct: its first-/second-order variance partition is not this endpoint fit.

Even symmetric subtraction is not exact:
\(d_i-r_i-c_i+\mu=e_i+(a_i+b_i)/(n-1)\). The correction matters particularly in
small pools. If all retrieval patterns are identical, template similarities may
vary with behavior while excess is zero. Correlating numerical remnants of that
zero vector would be misleading; separate component correlations return NA with
a constant-component reason.

## Raw performance retains the baseline

```{r raw}
raw <- summarize_era_endpoints(z)
raw$table
raw$identity_error
```

Raw means weight valid complete blocks by their item counts. Consequently,
mean(total) = mean(shared) + mean(excess), and mean(encoding) and mean(retrieval)
are structural zeros. Their tiny floating-point estimates must not be tested
against zero. The result marks structural/descriptive quantities and leaves
inferential fields NA. Invalid blocks are excluded explicitly, with counts and
zero raw weight; inspect those counts before combining participants.

Mean excess equals mean one-sided specificity **for the same complete pools and
item weights**. The addition is a trialwise allocation, not a new average
discrimination score under those conditions. Endpoint RMS measures the amplitude
of endpoint variation, includes estimation noise, and is not additive performance
or evidence of above-chance matching. Do not split the shared baseline into
arbitrary encoding and retrieval halves.

## Additive behavioral covariance

```{r behavior}
vividness <- setNames(rnorm(12), keys)
motion <- matrix(rnorm(24), 12, 2,
                 dimnames = list(keys, c("encoding_fd", "retrieval_fd")))
vividness[3] <- NA_real_
assoc <- summarize_era_endpoints(
  z, summary = "covariance_contributions", behavior = vividness,
  nuisance = motion, adjust_blocks = TRUE, cor_method = "spearman"
)
assoc$table
assoc$exclusions
assoc$identity_error
```

Endpoints are fitted to the prespecified full blocks **before** behavior/motion
subsetting. One common complete-case set and one nuisance projection H are then
used for every component and the behavior. The projection always includes an
intercept and, by default, competitor-block intercepts. Redundant nuisance
columns are handled by the same QR projection. Counts, exclusion reasons,
nuisance rank and residual degrees of freedom accompany the estimates.

For a component x, the signed contribution is

\[
C_x=\frac{(Hx)^\top(HV)}{\|Hd\|\,\|HV\|}.
\]

Thus the **Pearson** total correlation equals the sum of shared, encoding,
retrieval and excess contributions. Shared contributes only numerical roundoff
when H absorbs its block intercepts. With `adjust_blocks = FALSE`, its explicit
contribution must be kept. Contributions can cancel or exceed one in magnitude;
they are not unique variance percentages, semi-partial correlations, or
"percent of reactivation explained."

The separately named `correlation` column normalizes each component separately.
With `cor_method = "spearman"`, components and behavior are ranked before the
same nuisance projection (the supplied nuisance design itself is unchanged).
These correlations do **not** add. Contributions always use unranked scores.
Effectively constant components/behavior return NA correlations with reasons;
constant total or behavior also makes the common contribution denominator
undefined. `status` describes contributions; `correlation_status` describes
each separate correlation. The default numerical tolerance is recorded in the
fit. Endpoint means over a behavioral subset need not be zero; the returned
`subset_component_means` makes that distinction visible.

## Regional and searchlight models

Use the same keyed specification with either analysis family:

```{r model-examples, eval=FALSE}
endpoint_spec <- era_endpoint_spec(
  keys, pool, behavior = vividness, nuisance = motion,
  encoding_run = enc_run, retrieval_run = ret_run,
  return_items = TRUE
)
era <- era_rsa_model(
  dataset, design, key_var = ~ item, pairing = "one_to_one",
  era_simfun = "pearson", era_components = "item", endpoints = endpoint_spec,
  era_association_score = "joint_excess", era_correlates = ~ vividness
)
regional <- run_regional(era, region_mask)
regional$fits[[1]]$endpoints$decomposition$items
maps <- run_searchlight(era, radius = 5)
save_results(maps, "endpoint-maps")

feature <- feature_rsa_model(
  dataset, feature_design, crossval = folds, method = "ridge",
  endpoints = endpoint_spec, return_predictions = TRUE
)
feature_regions <- run_regional(feature, region_mask)
predictions <- feature_rsa_predictions(feature_regions)
feature_regions$fits[[1]]$endpoints$decomposition$items
```

ERA requires explicit one-to-one pairing for this opt-in path. Its ordinary
association formulas can select `era_association_score = "joint_excess"`;
the specification's behavior/nuisance summary separately emits all component
contributions and correlations. It need not use the same covariates as the
ordinary formula analysis, so record both estimands.

Feature scoring uses unchanged out-of-fold predictions and observed patterns.
Keys must match unique design labels, every design row must be assessed once,
and competitor blocks must be nested within outer assessment folds. A block
crossing folds is refused, not silently split. Use smaller, prespecified pools
within a fold if scientifically appropriate. No tuning on behavior occurs.
The `encoding` column now denotes a **predicted-template endpoint** and carries
`template_source = "held_out_prediction"` and the fold ledger. Retaining the
source prediction matrices is optional and supported for regional results;
searchlights require `return_predictions = FALSE` and discard item tables.

The built-in feature summaries compare predictions with the observed targets of
that feature fit. To address the cross-phase question with **predicted encoding
templates versus separate recall observations**, reuse the retained predictions
explicitly, without refitting or retuning the feature model:

```{r predicted-encoding-recall, eval=FALSE}
predicted_keys <- feature_design$labels[predictions$observation_index[[1]]]
stopifnot(identical(recall_voxel_index, predictions$voxel_index[[1]]))
predicted_era <- era_endpoint_decomposition(
  encoding = predictions$predicted[[1]], retrieval = recall_patterns,
  item_key = list(encoding = predicted_keys, retrieval = recall_item_key),
  competitor_block = pool, template_source = "held_out_prediction"
)
summarize_era_endpoints(predicted_era, "covariance_contributions",
                        behavior = vividness, nuisance = motion)
```

This requires exactly the same item set and voxel identities in the two phases;
the helper aligns the items by key. Keep the prediction fold ledger alongside
the result and prespecify pools nested within those folds. The standalone
provenance label does not itself verify training ancestry or held-out status.

Scalar names start with `era_endpoint_` or `feature_endpoint_`. They include
`mean_total`, `mean_shared`, `mean_encoding`, `mean_retrieval`, `mean_excess`,
`encoding_rms`, `retrieval_rms`, `n`, `n_excluded`, `n_blocks`, and `identity_error`.
Behavior adds `assoc_n`, `assoc_n_excluded`, `assoc_identity_error`,
`contribution_<component>` and `cor_<component>`. The total contribution is the
Pearson total association; the separate total correlation follows `cor_method`.
NIfTI exports retain structural NA values and local item counts. These counts
are not participant counts: group summaries must calculate the number of
participants with a finite value separately at each location and metric.

Model scoring sees the features supplied by the existing ROI extraction and
training-only filtering pipeline. Endpoint decomposition adds no across-item
mean subtraction or new feature screening. Direct helper comparisons must use
the same retained voxel set. Different filters or competitor pools change the
estimand and must be recorded.

## Interpretation and inference

Spatial centering per pattern, subtracting an across-item mean spatial pattern,
run nuisance handling, and endpoint decomposition are different operations. A
predictive across-item transformation must be estimated on training data only.
Endpoint decomposition changes the score interpretation; it cannot establish
that a GLM, timing alignment, mask, or experimental null is valid.

Use independent participants for group inference. Off-diagonal cells and
overlapping searchlights are not independent observations. Ordinary participant
means preserve the additive identities; separately Fisher-transforming
components does not. Test paired differences between contributions to compare
them, and test group differences directly instead of comparing significance
within groups. Specify multiplicity families for the scientific claim: pooled
FDR over strong baseline effects and excess is not necessarily more conservative
for excess than an excess-only family.

Endpoint permutations are not implemented by the feature model's existing
permutation outputs. A future permutation analysis must define whether it tests
behavioral labels, conditional pairing, or generalization to new items. Pairing
shuffles must respect pools, keep behavior attached to its observational unit,
and recompute the decomposition; learned models must be refitted when the null
requires it. Existing `nperm` outputs test only the legacy feature metrics.

Excess is correspondence beyond an additive endpoint model, not proof of an
exclusively item-specific or causal reinstatement mechanism. Nonadditive category
structure, estimation noise and misspecification can remain. Excluding diagonal
cells does not make endpoint estimation held-out across items: each item's
pattern still participates in nonmatch comparisons. Feature cross-validation is
a separate protection, whose provenance must also be retained.
